passage: Dolma and I share a hostel room, so I saw a lot of this. She lights a small butter lamp every morning and turns her prayer beads in the corridor before class. Some boys in the common room started calling her "superstitious" and asking if her lamp cured exams. I watched her go quiet and put the beads in her pocket. I can't say what she felt, though she skipped the common room for a week. Then Rahul, who has said openly that he doesn't believe in any gods, sat next to her and asked, "What do you say when you turn them?" Dolma explained, a little shy. He nodded and said, "I don't share it, but I get why it matters to you." The next morning she took out the beads in the corridor again. Neelam

qa.q: What does Dolma do every morning?
qa.a: Dolma lights a small butter lamp every morning and turns her prayer beads in the corridor before class.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling when she put the beads in her pocket?
qa.a: Dolma was probably hurt and self-conscious after being called superstitious, though Neelam cannot be sure what she felt inside.

qa.q: Which choice by Rahul changed things for Dolma?
qa.a: Rahul asked politely what she says when she turns the beads and listened, saying he doesn't share it but understands why it matters.

qa.q: How might Rahul see Dolma's prayer beads?
qa.a: As something he does not share but can respect. He asked what she says when she turns them and told her he gets why it matters to her.

grounding: A young person from a devout family is teased as superstitious, and a non-believing peer shows that respect can run in both directions.

passage: Monday. In the college canteen, three classmates laughed at Rekha, who fasts on Thursdays and wears a tulsi mala. "Still into that old stuff? So backward." Rekha smiled thinly and left her tea half finished. Wednesday. Rekha's friend Sunaina, who doesn't believe in God, sat down beside her. "I don't fast, but you're not stupid. You're thoughtful about it. Can I ask why Thursday?" Rekha explained that it was her grandmother's way and now hers, a day to slow down. Friday. When the teasing started again in the canteen, Sunaina said, "Some of us believe, some don't. Let's argue about ideas, not people." Rekha met her eye and smiled.

qa.q: What does Rekha do on Thursdays?
qa.a: Rekha fasts on Thursdays.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rekha felt hurt and embarrassed. She smiled thinly and left her tea half finished.

qa.q: Which choice by Sunaina on Wednesday changed things?
qa.a: Sunaina, who does not believe, said Rekha was not stupid and asked politely why Thursday, so Rekha could explain in her own words.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Rekha's fasting?
qa.a: As something thoughtful that comes from Rekha's grandmother's way. Sunaina does not share it but respects it, and says believers and non-believers can differ warmly.

grounding: A young person from a devout family is teased as backward, and a friend who does not believe shows respect running in both directions.

passage:
Exam week in the hostel, and the power had gone out again. Zubin, twenty, sat on his bed in the torch-light, retying the thin cord of his kusti around his waist as he did every morning and night.
From the next bed, someone snorted. "Still doing the magic string thing, Zubin? In the twenty-first century?" The others laughed.
Zubin's hands paused. His face went hot. He'd heard this before, since first year.
Then Hrithik, who didn't believe in anything and said so often, put down his notes. "Leave him. He sits with me every night explaining calculus. He's the most thoughtful guy on this floor."
"You don't even believe in God," someone said.
"No," Hrithik said. "And he does. We argue about it over chai. He's never once called me foolish."
Zubin finished the knot. Later, he offered Hrithik the last of his biscuits, and Hrithik took two.

qa.q: What was Zubin retying around his waist?
qa.a: He was retying the thin cord of his kusti around his waist.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when his hands paused?
qa.a: Zubin felt embarrassed and hurt, his face going hot, because he had been mocked about it since first year.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's reply show about respect?
qa.a: It shows respect running both ways: a non-believer can defend a believer, value his thoughtfulness, and disagree warmly over chai.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel about his friendship with Zubin?
qa.a: Hrithik seems to value it deeply, feeling respected because Zubin has never called him foolish for his own views.

grounding: In a hostel, a young man from a devout family is mocked as superstitious, and a non-believing friend shows that both can be thoughtful and differ warmly.

passage:
Every morning in the college hostel in Chennai, Anand, nineteen, drew a thin line of vibhuti on his forehead before class. By the second week, Pranav had a nickname for him: "Pandit-ji."
"Our physics genius still believes ash will help him pass," Pranav announced in the canteen. People laughed. Anand kept eating, but he started washing off the vibhuti before class.
A week later, Pranav was struggling with a lab report at midnight. Anand sat with him until two, patiently explaining every step.
At the end, Pranav said, "Why did you stop wearing the ash?"
Anand shrugged. "Got tired of the jokes."
Pranav was quiet. "I'm sorry. I thought believing meant not thinking. You clearly think more than me."
The next morning, the line of vibhuti was back. Pranav nodded at it, and said nothing.

qa.q: What nickname did Pranav give Anand?
qa.a: Pranav called him "Pandit-ji."

qa.q: Why did Anand start washing off the vibhuti before class?
qa.a: Anand felt embarrassed and tired of the jokes, so he hid a part of his faith to avoid being mocked.

qa.q: What changed Pranav's mind, and what could others learn from it?
qa.a: Anand's patient help showed Pranav that belief and careful thinking go together; others could learn not to judge a believer as foolish.

qa.q: How has Pranav's view of believers changed by the end?
qa.a: Pranav first saw belief as a lack of thinking, but after Anand's patient help he apologises and quietly accepts the vibhuti, seeing Anand as thoughtful.

grounding: A young man from a devout family is teased as superstitious, and his peer learns that a believer can be thoughtful, so respect runs both ways.

passage:
"Himani, you're fasting AGAIN? It's the third Navratri day. You know it doesn't actually do anything, right?"
"It does something for me, Pallavi."
"Like what? It's just superstition. You're a science student!"
"I'm also my Nani's granddaughter. We fast together every year. It makes me feel calm, and close to her."
"But you don't really think the goddess is watching you not eat?"
"I don't know exactly what I think. I pray, and it helps me. You don't, and you're fine. Why does it bother you?"
Pallavi paused. "I guess I thought smart people didn't believe."
"Then what does that make my Nani? She taught me maths before school did."
"...Okay. Fair. Sorry, that was rude."
"You're allowed to not believe. I'm allowed to fast. Now help me find somewhere that sells sabudana khichdi."
"Fine. And I'm eating a samosa next to you."
"Deal."

qa.q: Which day of Navratri is it?
qa.a: It's the third Navratri day.

qa.q: What does Himani feel when she fasts?
qa.a: Himani feels calm and close to her Nani.

qa.q: Which part of Himani's reply helped most, and why?
qa.a: Himani asked why her belief bothered Pallavi and pointed out that her Nani, who taught her maths, is thoughtful too, which made Pallavi rethink her assumption without a fight.

qa.q: How does Pallavi's view change during the conversation?
qa.a: Pallavi starts by calling fasting superstition, then realises she assumed smart people don't believe, apologises, and joins Himani warmly.

grounding: A young woman from a devout family is teased as superstitious by a friend, and they learn to differ warmly with respect in both directions.

passage: Our hostel wing had a running joke in first year: "Parul's asking her gods for marks again." I fast on Tuesdays and keep a small Hanuman picture on my desk, and Rukmini, my roommate, would strike a match near it and ask if he'd blow it out. People laughed. I laughed too, which I regret. Inside I felt small, as if my whole family was being called foolish. One night in October I told her so, straight, without crying. Rukmini didn't apologise at once. She said, "I really don't get it. Explain it to me?" So I did: my Nani, the fasting, how the quiet helps me study. She told me why she stopped believing at fourteen. We didn't agree. We still don't. But she hasn't touched a matchbox near my desk since, and on Tuesdays she saves me fruit.

qa.q: What did Rukmini say when Parul spoke to her in October?
qa.a: She said, "I really don't get it. Explain it to me?"

qa.q: How did Parul feel when the wing laughed at the jokes?
qa.a: Parul felt small and hurt, as if the whole family was being called foolish, even while laughing along.

qa.q: Why did Parul's way of speaking up work?
qa.a: Parul told Rukmini plainly and calmly how it felt, which invited questions instead of a fight, so they could each explain their views.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Parul's faith now?
qa.a: Rukmini still doesn't share it but seems to respect it, dropping the matchbox teasing and saving fruit for Parul on Tuesdays.

grounding: It illustrates a young person from a devout family teased as foolish, and how honest talk lets a believer and a non-believer differ warmly with respect both ways.
